extracted.intended_audience: Individuals and organizations preparing public comments on federal agency rulemakings (advocates, researchers, stakeholders, and members of the public)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting effective public comments to federal agency proposed rules, emphasizing strategy, specificity, originality, readability, citation, and procedural niceties to maximize influence. Focuses on crafting comments that agency staff (and contractors) can use in rulemaking records and analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess Your Strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Before submitting, evaluate whether a public comment best serves your goals. Agencies hold public meetings, request information on certain topics, react to pressure from U.S. legislators, and seek comment on guidelines and plans. Consider alternative engagement methods for your specific situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh other engagement options (e.g., public meetings, requests for information, legislative outreach, commenting on guidelines or plans) and match the channel to your objective rather than defaulting to filing a comment. If the rulemaking is not the best path to your goals, pursue those alternatives instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop Specific Arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid vague statements about general concepts. Instead, directly address the proposed rule with detailed reasoning and supporting evidence that agencies haven't already considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make concrete, rule-specific claims — cite the proposal text or sections and explain exactly how the rule is deficient or should be changed. Do not rely on broad assertions; show how the facts or law support your requested change and provide supporting data or analysis where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribute Original Insights
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit novel arguments, data, or analyses with technical and legal foundations. Keep content relevant to the specific rule—extraneous information may be overlooked. Review existing regulatory analyses (like Regulatory Impacts Analysis documents) to verify your arguments' validity and originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide new empirical evidence, technical analyses, or legal reasoning not already in the docket. Check the agency's regulatory impact analysis and other docket materials first so you avoid repeating points already considered; emphasize what is genuinely new and how it affects the agency's decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhance Readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Write clearly, recognizing that contractors using specialized software often review comments. Subtlety gets lost; explicit clarity increases comprehension and impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain language, clear structure, and explicit statements of your requested outcome. Avoid ambiguous phrasing and nuanced rhetoric that may be misinterpreted by reviewers or omitted by software; use headings, short paragraphs, and direct recommendations to improve uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference Specific Rule Sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly identify the section(s) of the rule your comment is addressing. Use Federal Register labels and features, or include section numbers and agency questions from the proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie each argument to the exact regulatory provision (e.g., cite Federal Register section labels or paragraph numbers and the agency's question identifiers). This helps reviewers place your comment in the record and ensures your point is associated with the correct part of the proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include Proper Citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Format references so staff can easily locate sources. Make non-accessible data publicly available through cited websites or attached files in accessible formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide full citations (URLs, document titles, dates, page or paragraph numbers) and, when citing non-public or large datasets, include accessible links or attach files in commonly used formats. Ensure supporting materials are discoverable by agency staff and contractors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate Your Comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass letter campaigns typically count as single submissions for consideration. Original comments have greater influence on specific rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever possible, submit individualized, substantive comments rather than form letters. Tailored comments are more likely to be treated separately in analyses and to affect specific regulatory text, whereas form letters may be aggregated and are less persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek Clarification
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact agency staff members listed in documents if you need rule explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parts of the proposal or the agency's analyses are unclear, reach out to the contact person named in the Federal Register notice or supporting documents to ask questions before submitting. Clarifying issues in advance can improve the precision and usefulness of your comment.
